rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Self-inductance L links a coil's flux to its own current, and the induced emf is −L dI/dt. It is zero for a steady current and it opposes any change. The stored energy is (1/2) L I^2.

Governing equation for "Self-induction and self-inductance" — state with units, then use in one numerical.
Φ = L I
Induced emf = −L dI/dt

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: A lamp in series with a coil lights slowly.  ·  The unit is the henry.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Self-induction is the emf induced in a coil by a change of its own current. The changing current changes the coil's own flux, and Faraday's law gives an emf.  ·  The self-inductance L is defined by NΦ = L I, so L is the flux linkage per unit current. The induced emf is −L dI/dt. The minus sign is Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change in current.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: A coil's own changing current induces an emf.  ·  L is the flux linkage per unit current.  ·  The emf opposes the change.  ·  L depends on turns, area and the core.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: When the current is increasing, the induced emf opposes the battery. When the current is decreasing, the induced emf tries to keep the current going. A spark at a switch is that attempt.  ·  L increases with more turns, a larger area, and an iron core. A long solenoid has L = μ0 n^2 A l, with n turns per unit length, if the field is the ideal solenoid field.  ·  The henry is the inductance that induces 1 V when the current changes at 1 A/s. Energy stored is (1/2) L I^2.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Self-inductance is not mutual inductance.  ·  The emf is zero when the current is steady, even if it is large.  ·  The minus sign is opposition, not a negative inductance.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Energy is (1/2) L I^2, not L I.  ·  Say whether the current is rising or falling before you say the direction.  ·  Use dI/dt in A/s.
